parts: So you test it.
You snap at Jay, your best friend.
Four. Three.
Two. One.
Her number does not move. Still three.
Sorry is just a word.
The number does not listen to words.
The numbers do not move.
Not one.
Good does not undo bad.
Good just waits.
You eat her leftovers.
The ones with her name on them.
She stops asking you for things.
She stops telling you things.
You watch her number like a clock.
Every mistake ticks it down.
But what would you say?
I can see your patience running out?
Science says a new habit takes sixty-six days.
Sixty-six days to build one good habit.
One bad moment takes one second.
That is the math. One second to break it.
Sixty-six days to rebuild it.
Day two: you walk your sister home.
Her number stays six.
Day three: you text Jay.
Just hey. No answer.
But something else does.
Your mom smiles when you come home.
Jay reads your text.
He does not reply. But he reads it.
Friday. The big game.
The whole school is there.
The one he told you in confidence.
The one about his dad leaving.
You say it like a joke.
The team laughs.
Jay hears it.
He is standing right behind you.
The pill does not turn red.
It does not flash. It just disappears.
Gone. Like he is gone.
He does not yell.
He does not hit you. He just walks away.
He does not answer your texts.
At school, he looks through you.
Zero does not mean angry.
Zero means done.
Done is quiet. Done does not slam doors.
Done just stops opening them.
One. Zero.
The pill is gone.
The old man does not shout.
He just sits down. He looks out the window.
He is used to it. That is the worst part.
He is used to being done with.
But you are the reason someone else looks like that now.
You get off the bus.
On your street, a couple argues on a porch.
Her number is four.
He says one more thing.
Four. Three. She turns away.
He stands there, hands in his pockets.
Nobody yells.
Nobody leaves. But something left anyway.
You keep walking. Every street has a number falling somewhere.
Every house. Every room.
You count them as you pass.
Eight. Six. Five. Three.
You check the mirror.
Your number was five.
Now it is four.
Four chances left with the people who matter.
You did not lose Jay's number.
You lost a piece of your own.
Then dinner.
Your mom asks about your day.
You snap at her.
You are tired. You are scared.
She goes quiet. Her number was three.
Now it is two. Two.
You watch it drop and you cannot stop it.
You say sorry. Sorry. Sorry.
The number does not move. It never moves up.
You go to your room.
You stare at the ceiling.
You have spent your whole life thinking people would always be there.
They will not.
Everyone has a number.
And every number is falling.
Tuesday.
You knock again. Nothing.
You keep going. You bring his homework.
You leave it at the door.
Day seven: rain.
You stand there anyway. Soaked.
Day eight: his little brother opens the door.
He just shakes his head.
Day nine: you leave a note.
Four words.
I was wrong. Forgive me later.
Day ten: you fix his bike chain.
It was rusted.
Day eleven: nothing.
You go anyway.
Showing up is not a trick.
It is not a key. It is just showing up.
It is Jay's mom.
She looks at you for a long time.
Then she says: he is in the backyard.
He sees you. He does not smile.
He does not walk away either.
He bounces the ball to you.
One bounce. That is all.
No number above his head. No pill.
Just a ball. Rolling to your feet.
And you understand. Zero was not the end.
Zero was the end of counting.
What comes after zero is not a number.
It is a choice. His choice. Not yours.
You pick up the ball.
You shoot. You miss.
He laughs. Just once.
Short. But it is real.
You play for an hour.
No one says sorry. No one has to.
That night you call your mom.
First. Every night now.
Your number never goes back up.
It stays four. It will always stay four.
The point is: you cannot earn a chance back.
You can only earn the next one.
So spend every chance like it is your last.
Because one day, it is.
You do not ask for a chance.
You do not say sorry. You just show up.
